title: Assessment of bioaerosol particle characteristics at different hospital wards and operating theaters: A case study in Tehran
author: Bolookat, Hassanvand, et al.

steps.title: Prepare culture media plates
steps.instruction: Obtain 90‑mm sterile Petri dishes and pour Tryptic cycloheximide soy agar for bacterial sampling and Sabouraud chloramphenicol dextrose agar for fungal sampling; allow agar to solidify.

steps.title: Label and arrange sampling plates
steps.instruction: Label each plate with site, date, and whether it is for bacterial or fungal analysis; prepare sets of plates for simultaneous bacterial and fungal sampling.

steps.title: Position plates for passive sampling
steps.instruction: From 10:00 AM to 16:00 PM, during the six‑month study period, place each labeled plate at a height of 1 m above the floor and at least 1 m away from walls, doors, windows, and any barriers, following the 1/1/1 scheme, and leave the plates exposed for exactly 1 hour.

steps.title: Collect plates after exposure
steps.instruction: At the end of the 1‑hour exposure, carefully retrieve the Petri dishes and transport them immediately to the laboratory for incubation.

steps.title: Incubate bacterial plates
steps.instruction: Incubate the bacterial plates at 37 ± 1 °C for 2 days.

steps.title: Incubate fungal plates
steps.instruction: Incubate the fungal plates at 25 ± 1 °C for 4 days.

steps.title: Record bed numbers and metadata
steps.instruction: For each sampling day and site, observe and record the number of active patient beds; also note the sampling time, location, and any deviations.

steps.title: Enumerate colonies and calculate IMA
steps.instruction: After incubation, count colony‑forming units (CFU) on each plate; compute the Index of Microbial Air contamination (IMA) as CFU / (m² · h) using the plate area (90 mm diameter) and the 1‑hour exposure time.

steps.title: Perform statistical analysis
steps.instruction: Using Minitab software version 17, calculate descriptive statistics, conduct one‑way ANOVA to compare bacterial, fungal, and total bioaerosol concentrations across sites, and apply simple linear regression to assess the relationship between number of beds and bioaerosol levels; consider p < 0.05 as significant.

description: Exposure to bioaerosols, as an important class of particulate matter (PM), have become one of the most issues in indoor air quality (IAQ) topics for occupational and public health [[1], [2], [3], [4]]. In particular, hospitals have a more complex and different environment rather than other occupational or residential ones. This is due to continuous working cycle, and special types of air pollutants, including pathogenic and chemical or biological agents [5]. Bioaerosols can originate from humans (including patients), various indoor hospital characteristics, and outdoor environmental sources [2]. It has been found that about 5–34% of indoor air pollution in different indoor environments such as hospitals, dentist ofﬁces, shopping centers, subway systems, public libraries, and other workplaces can be attributable to bioaerosols, particularly bacterial and fungal bioaerosols [3,6]. Bioaerosols are compounds with biological origin, including dead or live bacterial and fungal spores, bacterial peptidoglycans and endotoxins, fungal mycotoxins and β (1, 3)-glucans, viruses, pollen grains, airborne algae, plant debris, and fragments of microbial insects, fur ﬁbres and skin fragments from animals and humans [[7], [8], [9]]. Among this wide range of species, bacterial and fungal aerosols have been introduced as the most important bioaerosols [3]. Bioaerosols in general, have been associated to several adverse health effects. Considering the significance of this issue, the World Health Organization (WHO) published a guideline on IAQ, in 2009 [10]. Well-documented environmental health studies demonstrate that exposure to bioaerosols, exceeding maximum acceptable levels can lead to non-infectious diseases, infectious diseases, including nosocomial infections or healthcare associated infections, acute toxic effects, cancer and even death, especially for immunosuppressed persons [1,[11], [12], [13], [14], [15], [16], [17], [18]].
